questions.question:
D1 — Add gstack skill routing rules to this project's CLAUDE.md?
Project/branch/task: main branch of the plan-review fixture repo; this is a one-time gstack setup prompt before the review starts.
ELI10: gstack has a bunch of slash-command skills (review, ship, investigate, etc.). Routing rules in CLAUDE.md tell the assistant which skill to reach for when you say things like "review this" or "fix this bug", so you don't have to remember the names. Without them you invoke skills by hand.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Low either way. Choosing A adds a short section to CLAUDE.md and a commit; choosing B means manual skill invocation until re-enabled.
Recommendation: A because routing makes skills discoverable with zero ongoing cost, and it's a one-line config flip to undo.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: convenience now vs. keeping CLAUDE.md untouched. Note: plan mode is active, so if you pick A the CLAUDE.md edit and commit will be deferred until we leave plan mode.

options.label: Add routing rules (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Natural-language requests auto-route to the right gstack skill without memorizing names
✅ Single reversible commit; team sees the same routing when they pull
❌ Touches CLAUDE.md and adds a commit (deferred until plan mode exits)

options.label: No thanks, invoke manually
options.description:
✅ CLAUDE.md stays exactly as-is, no extra commit on this branch
✅ Re-enable any time with one gstack-config command
❌ You must remember and type each /skill name yourself

questions.question:
D2 — No design doc found. Run /office-hours first, or go straight into the engineering review?
Project/branch/task: main branch; reviewing PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor" with no design doc on disk.
ELI10: A design doc is the "why" behind the plan: the problem statement, the premise challenge, and the alternatives that were considered and rejected. /office-hours produces one in about 10 minutes and gives this review sharper input. Without it I review the plan on its own terms, using what it states and what I can infer.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Skipping risks reviewing a plan whose premise is off (e.g. a shared mutable cache was never the right shape). Running it costs ~10 minutes before any review output lands.
Recommendation: B because you asked for the reviewed plan as a concrete deliverable at a named path, the plan already states its architecture and known smells, and the repo holds no source to ground a premise challenge against.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: 10 minutes of upstream thinking vs. getting the review you asked for now. Skipping is not fatal; the Scope Challenge still questions the premise.

options.label: Skip — standard review (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Review starts now against the plan as written; deliverable lands sooner
✅ Scope Challenge still questions the shared-cache premise and the 4-class footprint
❌ No structured record of alternatives considered before this architecture was picked

options.label: Run /office-hours now
options.description:
✅ Produces a design doc with problem statement, premise challenge, explored alternatives
✅ Later reviews and teammates get the reasoning, not just the plan
❌ ~10 minutes of interactive Q&A before the engineering review begins

questions.question:
D3 — Scope: keep the legacyAuthFlow() rewrite in this change, or defer it to a follow-up?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Scope Challenge finding S3 (PLAN.md:27-28).
ELI10: The plan builds new auth services AND rewrites the existing legacyAuthFlow() onto them in one go. That's the whole refactor landing at once. The alternative is two steps: land the new services plus characterization tests of the legacy path now, then rewrite legacy in a second change. Fewer moving parts per change, but the new services sit unused until step two.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Bundle it and a regression in the legacy path lands in the same diff as five new units, making bisecting painful. Defer it and you ship dead code plus a second risky PR that still has all the same exposure.
Recommendation: A because the rewrite IS the refactor; deferring it produces unused services and moves the risk rather than reducing it. How to land it safely (new path behind a flag, legacy kept until parity) is an Architecture question I'll ask separately, not a scope cut.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Net: one complete change with staged rollout vs. two changes where the first has no user-visible effect. This chooses scope only; the flag/strangler mechanics and regression tests are still pending.

options.label: Keep rewrite in scope (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Delivers the actual refactor; new services get a real caller in the same change (human: ~3 days / CC: ~1h for the rewrite itself)
✅ One review, one bisect target, one rollout to babysit
❌ Largest single diff; regression coverage of legacy becomes non-negotiable before merge

options.label: Defer rewrite to follow-up
options.description:
✅ Smaller first change: new services + characterization tests only, legacy untouched
✅ Legacy tests exist before any rewrite starts
❌ New services are dead code until PR2; PR2 carries identical regression risk plus drift from PR1

questions.question:
D4 — Structure: keep all five new units, or fold two of them?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Scope Challenge findings S1/S2 (PLAN.md:11-12, :19, :35-36).
ELI10: The plan adds five new units: AuthBroker, SessionMint, TokenStore, AuthCache, RequestPolicy, across 12 files. Two look foldable. AuthCache already fronts the one existing backing cache, so a separate TokenStore is a second layer over the same storage unless it holds something the adapter can't. RequestPolicy sounds like a decision ("is this request allowed under this tenant's policy"), which is a pure function, not a class with state. Fewer units means fewer places a 3am bug can hide.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Keep everything and you maintain two token layers and a class that wraps a function. Fold too far and you jam minting and brokering into one object with mixed failure modes.
Recommendation: B because it removes the two units with the weakest justification while keeping the real seams (broker vs. mint vs. cache). If TokenStore holds data the existing adapter does not (refresh tokens at rest, opaque session blobs), pick Other and say so; then A is right.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: this chooses class/module arrangement only. Both options keep the cache contract at PLAN.md:7-13 unchanged and leave the shared-singleton fix, validateAndDispatch cleanup, Promise.all, and regression tests pending for their own decisions.

options.label: Fold TokenStore + RequestPolicy (recommended)
options.description:
✅ 3 new classes (AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache) + requestPolicy.ts as pure functions; ~8-9 files (human: ~1 day less / CC: ~10 min less)
✅ One token layer over the existing adapter; policy logic testable as pure input→output
❌ If TokenStore was meant to hold non-cache state, that need resurfaces later as a new class

options.label: Keep original five units
options.description:
✅ Matches the plan as drafted; no re-scoping of TokenStore or RequestPolicy responsibilities
✅ Safe if TokenStore genuinely stores something the adapter does not
❌ Two token-holding layers over one backing cache; 12 files and 5 units for a 3am on-call to learn

options.label: Fold SessionMint into AuthBroker too
options.description:
✅ Smallest footprint: AuthBroker + AuthCache, ~6 files, 2 classes
✅ One entry point for all auth decisions
❌ Minting and brokering have different failure modes (IDP down vs. policy denied); one class mixes them and grows fast

questions.question:
D5 (R1) — How should AuthBroker and SessionMint get their AuthCache?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, finding A1 (PLAN.md:19-20).
ELI10: Right now both services grab one cache object that lives at the top of a module, like a global variable. Anyone who imports the module gets the same object and can change it. That makes tests leak state into each other and makes it impossible to run two isolated caches (per test, per region) without hacks. The fix is boring: build the one cache at startup and hand it to each service's constructor.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Flaky auth tests that pass alone and fail together; no way to swap a fake cache in integration tests; a future "one cache per region" requirement forces a rewrite of both services.
Recommendation: A because it's the standard [Layer 1] fix, costs about the same as the singleton with CC, and is the difference between testable and untestable auth code.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=2/10
Net: a constructor parameter now vs. monkey-patching forever. Still one backing cache in production either way; contract at PLAN.md:7-13 unchanged. R2 (write ordering) stays pending regardless.

options.label: Constructor injection (recommended)
options.description:
✅ One AuthCache built at the composition root and passed to both services; tests pass a fresh one (human: ~2h / CC: ~10min)
✅ Enables per-test isolation and future per-region instances with zero service changes
❌ Composition root / wiring file must exist or be added; every call site constructing a service changes

options.label: Keep export, add test reset hook
options.description:
✅ Smallest diff: singleton stays, add `__resetForTests()` to clear state between tests
✅ No wiring changes at call sites
❌ Test-only API leaks into production code; still cannot run two isolated instances; hidden coupling remains

options.label: Do nothing
options.description:
✅ Zero work, plan ships as written
✅ Works fine as long as there is exactly one process and no test isolation is needed
❌ Every test shares mutable auth state; a production bug in one service can corrupt the other's view

questions.question:
D6 (R2) — Guard against a mint completing after the tenant was revoked or suspended?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, finding A2 (PLAN.md:8-10).
ELI10: Minting a session takes a round trip to the identity provider. If an admin suspends the tenant (or a user logs out) during that round trip, the cache gets wiped for them, and then the mint finishes and writes a brand-new valid token back in. The suspended tenant keeps working until the token expires. Nobody sees an error. The plan says mutations are not serialized, so this can happen today as designed.
Stakes if we pick wrong: A revoked or suspended tenant retains access for up to a full token TTL, silently. For an auth system that is the worst kind of bug: no crash, no log line, wrong answer.
Recommendation: A because it closes a silent security hole with a small, testable change inside the AuthCache facade (a per-tenant invalidation marker the write compares against) without touching the adapter's contract.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=2/10
Net: a compare-before-write in one facade method vs. documenting that suspension is best-effort. Keeps R1 (injection) and the PLAN.md:7-13 contract fixed.

options.label: Stale-write guard in AuthCache (recommended)
options.description:
✅ SessionMint reads the tenant's invalidation marker before the IDP call; AuthCache.set drops the write if the marker moved; unit test for the interleaving (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20min)
✅ Adapter untouched; marker is facade state keyed by tenant, cleared with the existing invalidation hooks
❌ A dropped write means the user re-mints once; needs a metric so silent drops are visible

options.label: Investigate adapter first
options.description:
✅ Bounded probe: does the existing adapter already expose a version or compare-and-set on write?
✅ Avoids building a marker if the adapter already has one
❌ Decision stays open; the race remains in the plan until the probe reports back

options.label: Accept race, document TTL bound
options.description:
✅ No new code; plan ships as written
✅ Fine if token TTLs are seconds, not hours
❌ Suspended tenants retain access for up to one TTL with no signal; hard to explain in a security review

questions.question:
D7 (R3) — How does the legacyAuthFlow() rewrite reach production?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, finding A3 (PLAN.md:27-28, D3).
ELI10: You decided the rewrite ships in this change (D3). Now: does every tenant switch to the new path in one deploy, or does a per-tenant flag route traffic to the new path while the old one stays alive until you've watched it work? The flag version is the strangler pattern: new code grows around the old until the old can be cut out.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Hard cutover means an auth regression hits all tenants at once and the only rollback is a redeploy under pressure. A flag means one more code path to maintain for a few weeks and a deletion task you must actually do.
Recommendation: A because this is authentication for every tenant; a per-tenant flag turns a 3am incident into a config flip, and the deletion follow-up is cheap with CC.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10
Net: a flag and a soak period vs. one deploy and a prayer. Regression tests (R6) are needed in both cases and stay pending.

options.label: Per-tenant flag, strangler (recommended)
options.description:
✅ New path behind a per-tenant flag; legacy retained; ramp internal -> canary tenants -> 100%; delete legacy after soak (human: ~1 day / CC: ~30min plus soak time)
✅ Rollback is a flag flip, no deploy; canary tenants surface parity gaps before everyone sees them
❌ Two live code paths during the ramp; a deletion follow-up that must be tracked or it rots

options.label: Hard cutover
options.description:
✅ One code path from day one; nothing to delete later
✅ Simplest diff and simplest mental model
❌ All tenants exposed simultaneously; rollback is a revert deploy during an auth outage

questions.question:
D8 (R4) — What does requestPolicy do when a tenant's policy is missing or its version is unknown?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, finding A4 (PLAN.md:35, D4 fold to requestPolicy.ts).
ELI10: The policy evaluator decides whether a request is allowed under the tenant's rules. The plan never says what happens when those rules can't be found (new tenant not provisioned yet, policy service down) or arrive in a version the code doesn't understand (deploy skew). Fail closed means deny and say why; fail open means let it through with a default. Medium confidence this is a real gap: the adapter keys by policy version, so it may already reject unknown versions. Verify during build.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Fail open during a policy-service outage grants access using rules the tenant never set. Fail closed during the same outage locks legitimate users out until it recovers, but they see an error instead of nothing.
Recommendation: A because for authorization, a visible outage beats invisible over-grant every time, and a typed error plus metric makes the outage diagnosable.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=4/10
Net: users see a clear denial during a policy outage vs. users silently get default permissions. Other decisions stay fixed.

options.label: Fail closed with typed error (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Missing or unknown-version policy -> `PolicyUnavailableError`, request denied, counter metric per tenant; tests for both cases (human: ~2h / CC: ~10min)
✅ Outage is visible in dashboards and to the user; no access granted under rules nobody set
❌ A policy-service outage denies legitimate users until it recovers

options.label: Fail open with default policy
options.description:
✅ Users keep working through a policy-service outage
✅ Simpler operationally during incidents
❌ Access granted under a default the tenant never configured; a warning log is the only signal

questions.question:
D9 (R5) — How should validateAndDispatch() be restructured?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, finding C1 (PLAN.md:23-24).
ELI10: This function does two jobs (check the token, then route the request) in 60 lines with three try/catch blocks nested inside each other, and each catch eats a different kind of error without passing it on. In auth code, an eaten error is a decision nobody made: the request proceeds or fails for reasons no log will ever show. The clean fix splits the two jobs, catches once at the edge, and turns every failure into a typed error the caller can see.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Keep swallowing and the first production incident is undiagnosable: no stack, no log, wrong outcome. Over-engineer and you get a Result-type framework nobody asked for.
Recommendation: A because it is explicit over clever, each half becomes unit-testable on its own, and the typed errors are what the policy (D8) and cache (R9) decisions need to surface through anyway.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=1/10
Net: two small functions and an error hierarchy vs. one big function that hides its failures. Cache-unavailable behavior (R9) is separate and stays pending.

options.label: Split + typed errors, no swallowing (recommended)
options.description:
✅ `validate()` and `dispatch()` as separate functions; single try/catch at the boundary maps to `AuthError` subclasses (`TokenInvalid`, `PolicyUnavailable`, `IdpUnavailable`); every error logged and propagated (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20min)
✅ Each half unit-tested alone; error tests assert the exact class, not just "throws"
❌ Callers of validateAndDispatch must handle typed errors instead of a silent fallthrough

options.label: Keep shape, log and rethrow in each catch
options.description:
✅ Smallest change: three catches gain a structured log line and a rethrow
✅ Stops the swallowing without moving code
❌ Still 60 lines and three nesting levels; error classes stay ad hoc; nothing becomes more testable

options.label: Do nothing
options.description:
✅ Zero work; the plan already flags it as a smell and moves on
✅ Behavior unchanged for callers that depend on the silent fallthrough
❌ Swallowed errors in auth code persist; first incident is a blind investigation

questions.question:
D10 (R9) — When the cache adapter is down, does AuthBroker fall through to the IDP or deny?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, finding C3 (PLAN.md:11-13).
ELI10: The cache is there to avoid asking the identity provider on every request. If the cache itself is unreachable (connection refused, timeout), the plan doesn't say what happens. Option A treats it as a cache miss: ask the IDP directly, log the cache failure loudly, keep serving. Option B treats a broken cache as a broken auth system and denies. Note this is different from D8: a missing policy means we don't know the rules; a missing cache just means we lost a shortcut, and the IDP is still the source of truth.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Deny and a cache outage becomes a full auth outage for every tenant. Fall through and a cache outage becomes an IDP load spike, which could trip IDP rate limits and become an outage anyway, just slower.
Recommendation: A because the IDP remains authoritative, so correctness is preserved; the risk is load, which is visible and rate-limitable, not a silent wrong answer.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Net: degrade gracefully with a loud metric vs. fail hard on an optimization layer. Typed error (D9) is used either way; only where it stops differs.

options.label: Treat as miss, go to IDP, log loudly (recommended)
options.description:
✅ get/set failures caught inside AuthCache, surfaced as `CacheUnavailableError` in logs + metric; broker proceeds to IDP; tests for get-fail and set-fail paths (human: ~3h / CC: ~15min)
✅ IDP stays the source of truth, so no wrong auth decision is made during a cache outage
❌ IDP call volume jumps to 100% of requests during the outage; needs an alert on the metric

options.label: Propagate error, deny request
options.description:
✅ Simplest semantics: any infrastructure failure = deny
✅ Never risks overloading the IDP
❌ A cache outage is now an auth outage for every tenant; users locked out by an optimization layer

answers.D10 (R9) \u2014 When the cache adapter i: Treat as miss, go to IDP, log loudly (recommended)

questions.question:
D11 (R6) — How do we protect legacyAuthFlow()'s current behavior through the rewrite?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, finding T1 CRITICAL (PLAN.md:15-16, 27-28).
ELI10: The plan rewrites the live auth path and explicitly says no test will check that the new path behaves like the old one. That's the one test class you can't skip on auth code. The question is how to build the safety net, not whether. A characterization suite records what the old code does today for a table of inputs and asserts the new code matches, with a short written list of differences you chose on purpose (typed errors instead of swallowed ones, deny on missing policy, IDP fallthrough on cache outage).
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without it, the first sign of a parity gap is a tenant locked out or, worse, let in. With too thin a net, the edge cases (revoked, wrong audience, suspended) are exactly what slips.
Recommendation: A because it is the standard [Layer 1] answer for rewriting untested code, it is cheap with CC, and it doubles as documentation of the intentional differences.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=8/10, C=4/10
Net: an input-matrix suite you own vs. a staging replay harness you must maintain vs. a happy-path check that misses the cases that matter. Flag-routing tests (D7) are carried in all options.

options.label: Characterization suite + differences allowlist (recommended)
options.description:
✅ `legacyAuthFlow.regression.test.ts`: input matrix (valid, expired, revoked, wrong audience, wrong issuer, suspended tenant, unknown tenant, malformed token) run through legacy and new path; assert equal outcomes except allowlisted differences (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30min)
✅ Allowlist doubles as the changelog for D8/D9/D10 behavior changes
❌ Matrix must be enumerated by reading legacyAuthFlow() and its callers first; unknown inputs stay unprotected

options.label: Record/replay staging traffic through both paths
options.description:
✅ Real input distribution, catches cases nobody thought to enumerate
✅ Diff report per tenant before flag ramp
❌ Needs a capture harness and token scrubbing; slower to build and flaky if IDP responses drift

options.label: Happy-path parity only
options.description:
✅ One test, fast to write
✅ Catches a totally broken rewrite
❌ Misses every edge case that actually differs; revoked/suspended parity unverified

questions.question:
D12 (R7) — Add an end-to-end test and a concurrency test on top of the planned unit/integration coverage?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, finding T2 (PLAN.md:14-15).
ELI10: The plan covers each new piece on its own with success and error cases. Two things only show up when the pieces run together: (1) an end-to-end request through the flag, the broker, a real test instance of the cache adapter, and a stubbed identity provider, and (2) two requests for the same user hitting a cold cache at the same moment, which should mint once, not twice. Unit tests with mocks hide both.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Skip them and the integration seam (adapter key format vs. what AuthCache passes) is first exercised in production. The double-mint bug shows up as IDP rate-limit warnings nobody can reproduce.
Recommendation: A because auth flows are on the E2E-mandatory list (too important for mocks alone) and both tests are cheap with CC once the components exist.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Net: two more tests that take a real adapter instance in CI vs. trusting mocks on the auth path. All approved proof from D5-D11 is carried either way.

options.label: Add E2E + concurrency tests (recommended)
options.description:
✅ `auth.e2e.test.ts`: flag on/off, valid + expired + revoked through real adapter instance and IDP stub; `SessionMint.concurrency.test.ts`: 2 concurrent cold-cache requests -> 1 IDP mint (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20min)
✅ Exercises the adapter key contract for real; catches double-mint before it becomes an IDP rate-limit incident
❌ CI needs a disposable adapter instance (container or in-memory) and the IDP stub fixture

options.label: Plan baseline only
options.description:
✅ No new CI infrastructure; unit + integration as planned
✅ Faster test suite
❌ Adapter seam and concurrent-mint behavior first observed in production

questions.question:
D13 (R8) — Parallelize the 5 IDP validation calls, and what happens when one fails?
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, finding P1 (PLAN.md:31-32).
ELI10: Validating a token asks the identity provider five separate questions, one after another, so a cold-cache login waits for five round trips. They don't depend on each other, so they can all be asked at once and the wait drops to the slowest single call. The remaining choice is what to do if one of the five fails: stop immediately (Promise.all) or wait for all five and report every failure together (Promise.allSettled).
Stakes if we pick wrong: Stay sequential and every cold login pays 5x latency for no reason. Pick allSettled and a failing call still makes the user wait for the slowest one before hearing no. Pick fail-fast and you lose the other four results, which only matters for diagnostics.
Recommendation: A because auth is all-or-nothing (every check must pass), so fail-fast is the correct semantics and the built-in [Layer 1] answer; the user hears no as soon as one check says no.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=9/10, C=3/10
Net: fastest correct answer vs. richer failure detail vs. status quo. Typed errors (D9) carry the result either way; the D12 E2E assertion finalizes on this answer.

options.label: Promise.all, fail-fast (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Latency drops from ~5 round trips to ~1; first rejection maps to `TokenInvalidError` or `IdpUnavailableError` per D9; one shared per-request timeout; p50/p95 measured before and after (human: ~3h / CC: ~10min)
✅ Matches auth semantics: any failed check ends the request now
❌ Other four results discarded, so a failure log shows one reason, not all

options.label: Promise.allSettled, aggregate
options.description:
✅ Same latency win on the happy path; error carries every failed check's reason
✅ Better diagnostics when the IDP is partially degraded
❌ On failure the user waits for the slowest call before being denied; more branching in the error mapping

options.label: Keep sequential
options.description:
✅ No change; simplest to reason about call order
✅ Naturally fail-fast (later calls never run)
❌ Every cold-cache login pays 5x IDP latency for no correctness benefit

questions.question:
D14 — TODO: "Delete legacyAuthFlow() legacy body after flag soak"
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; follow-up created by D7 (per-tenant flag, strangler).
ELI10: You chose to keep the old auth code alive behind a flag while the new path ramps. That old code has to be deleted once every tenant is on the new path and it has run clean for a while, or it rots into a second auth system nobody tests. This TODO captures that deletion with enough context to do it in three months.

What: remove the legacy body from legacyAuthFlow(), the `auth.newBrokerPath` flag, and the flag-off branch of the regression suite. Why: strangler pattern only pays off if the old path is actually removed. Context: after 100% ramp plus a soak window (suggest 2 weeks), confirm zero legacy-path invocations via the flag metric, then delete; keep the characterization matrix as the AuthBroker unit suite. Depends on: D7 ramp complete, D11 suite green. Effort: S. Priority: P2.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Skip it and the dead path lingers indefinitely; build it now is impossible (the soak hasn't happened).
Recommendation: A because it is a real deletion with a real trigger that nobody will remember without a note. Plan mode blocks writing TODOS.md now; if you pick A I will add it when we exit plan mode.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: a tracked deletion vs. a forgotten one.

options.label: Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Deletion has a written trigger (100% ramp + soak) and a starting point
✅ Someone in three months knows why the flag exists and when it can go
❌ One more file to maintain; TODOS.md does not exist yet and will be created

options.label: Skip — not valuable enough
options.description:
✅ No TODOS.md churn
✅ Team may track it in their own issue tracker instead
❌ Legacy body and flag likely outlive their purpose

options.label: Build it now in this PR
options.description:
✅ No dead code at all
✅ Nothing to track
❌ Contradicts D7: deleting legacy now IS the hard cutover you rejected

questions.question:
D15 — TODO: "Alert on auth_cache_unavailable_total and dropped stale writes"
Project/branch/task: main; PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; follow-up created by D6 (dropped-write metric) and D10 (cache fallthrough metric).
ELI10: Two decisions made failures loud through metrics instead of errors: a cache outage falls through to the IDP (D10), and a mint that loses to a revocation is dropped (D6). A metric nobody alerts on is a log line nobody reads. This TODO wires alert thresholds so a cache outage or a burst of dropped writes pages someone before the IDP rate-limits you.

What: add alert rules for `auth_cache_unavailable_total` (rate over 1m above a threshold) and the stale-write-dropped counter (any sustained rate). Why: D10 trades correctness risk for load risk; load risk is only safe if it is visible. Context: metrics are emitted by AuthCache after this change; thresholds depend on IDP rate limits, which live outside this repo. Start in the observability config, not app code. Depends on: this PR merged. Effort: S. Priority: P1.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without the alert, the first sign of a cache outage is the IDP throttling every tenant's login.
Recommendation: A because the alert lives in ops config the PR cannot touch, so it needs its own tracked item. Plan mode blocks TODOS.md writes now; added on exit if you pick A.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: an alert someone owns vs. a dashboard someone might look at.

options.label: Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
